content.introduction: For 2026, a practical asset allocation strategy could spread investments across equity, debt, gold, and cash with a balanced portfolio holding around 50–60% equity, 25–30% debt, 10% gold, and 5% cash. Long-term investors may consider a higher equity allocation. Gold is recommended to hold 10–15% for diversification and as a hedge. Institutional asset owners are planning to add to hedge funds, infrastructure, private credit, private equity, non-US developed market equities, emerging market equities, and return-seeking fixed income, while reducing large-cap US equities. The Wellington Solutions team maintains a moderately overweight view on global equities, preferring Japan and the US over Europe and emerging markets. Active ETFs may offer a tax-efficient way to rotate holdings with evolving macro and micro dynamics.
body:
A practical asset allocation strategy for 2026 can spread investments across equity, debt, gold and cash based on your goals and time horizon. A balanced portfolio could hold around 50–60% equity, 25–30% debt, 10% gold and 5% cash, while long-term investors may take a higher equity allocation.

### 2. How much gold should you hold in your portfolio in 2026? [...] For an asset allocation strategy for 2026, a 10–15% gold allocation can provide diversification and act as a hedge when other parts of the portfolio come under pressure. The article recommends treating gold as a permanent allocation rather than trying to time its price.

### 3. How often should you rebalance your portfolio? [...] Most years, you can get away with owning one thing. 2026 has not been one of those years. An asset allocation strategy for 2026 matters because equity, debt, gold and cash have behaved very differently this year. A simple mix across these four buckets can help you manage volatility, protect money needed for near-term goals and still give your portfolio room to grow.

Turning to long-term portfolio opportunities, we found in a recent poll we conducted (Figure 4) that the top areas institutional asset owners were planning to add to in 2026 included hedge funds, infrastructure, private credit, private equity, non-US developed market equities, emerging market equities, and return-seeking fixed income. The area they were most likely to reduce was, by far, large-cap US equities.

View More [...] Dynamic fixed income strategies — Total-return-oriented, opportunistic, and multisector strategies could all be well positioned to navigate relatively tight spreads and low interest rates and to pivot as market opportunities emerge.
 Hedge funds — More dispersion in economic outcomes (think about China versus Japan versus Europe today) and security-level results could benefit hedge funds, including multi-strategy, macro, and equity long/short strategies. [...] Our Wellington Solutions team maintains a 6- to 12-month outlook for tactical asset allocation purposes. As of December 2025, they have a moderately overweight view on global equities. While valuations are high, equity returns should benefit from lower global economic policy uncertainty, which has declined since the tariff-driven peak in April 2025, and central bank easing. Investors are paying more attention to AI as it encompasses a growing share of traditional asset classes in their portfolios. Within equity sleeves, dividends and quality stocks can prove useful diversifiers, while looking beyond IG credit can limit a bond allocation’s correlation to equities. Investors may look outside of stocks and bonds to alternatives or commodity strategies that historically have been negatively correlated with equities to seek additional diversification. [...] In its June index reconstitution, FTSE Russell moved many of the market’s AI and semiconductor momentum leaders more squarely into Growth, making the style a cleaner expression of the AI earnings story.25 Shifting momentum and style leadership this year underwrites our preference for dynamic allocation strategies rather than static holdings. Active ETFs may offer a tax-efficient way to rotate holdings with evolving macro and micro dynamics without the need for frequent portfolio rebalancing.
